name: A playable world model of the Backrooms
description:
A 211M-param transformer acts as a game engine. It draws every next frame from the last 2.4 seconds and my inputs.

Built a simulator of 18 Backrooms levels in PyTorch to generate the data.

Recorded 440 hours of scripted play in it.

Trained the model from scratch on that, using flow matching in a pretrained autoencoder's latent space.

The model was trained on its own imperfect frames as context so it doesn't drift right away. It recalls a few older frames by position, so a quick look back usually works.

Inspired by Oasis Minecraft.

To try it you need an NVIDIA GPU with ~4 GB.

Weights: https://huggingface.co/yelarys/noclip

Video with sound: https://x.com/yelaryss

name: Quadrivia – Trivia for the Intellectually Curious
description:
I made Quadrivia, a trivia game covering science, math, logic, nature, geography, and philosophy.

I had the idea about ten years ago. I like trivia, but I don't know much about pop culture, so I wanted a game built for subjects I enjoy. I started writing down questions in my phone's Notes app and reading them to my friends. That eventually became this app.

I put a ton of care into the question creation. The questions are the game. Some reward knowing something interesting, whilst others give you a foothold to reason toward the answer. Building that balance is the hardest part, but when you see the a-ha moment on players faces you begin to understand why the question design is so important.

The game can be played solo but is meant to be played with friends around a table or over FaceTime. You earn "citations" across fields of knowledge and the first to an h-index of 4 wins the game.

The app is free to download with a started question set that supports complete games.

If you're interested in the name: Trivia comes from "Trivium" which in Medieval education were the three foundational subjects (Grammar, Logic, and Rhetoric). Similarly, Quadrivia comes from "Quadrivium" which in Roman times referred to the four mathematical disciplines (Arithmetic, Music, Geometry, and Astronomy).

name: It's now easy to install Linux on an Android Phone – Android2linux
description:
Hey HN!

One of my biggest dreams (really) was to have a Linux phone. I tried to install on some phones in the past, even the ones that would be marked as compatible and it was always so difficult that I couldn't really do it. Yesterday I decided to try again, this time using Claude to do most of the work. A couple hours later it runs postmarketOS as my second phone: 4G, SMS, a terminal, SSH.

It took two fixes. U-Boot didn't recognise my phone model, so I patched 14 bytes of its device-tree match strings. Then the modem wasn't working, because the packaged TFTP server that lends the modem a folder mishandled its file-size queries but an upstream build fixed it.

The repo is what came out of it: guides for any phone (but specific just for my xiaomi), an agent skill that follows the same method and safety rules, notes per phone, and web apps reworked for a phone screen (WhatsApp Web for desktop with a one-pane layout).

What doesn't work (in this phone of mine): no charger driver yet (slow charging), no cameras, and no banking apps, so I keep an Android at home for those. Whether this works for you depends on your phone having a port. reports through the issue forms help, especially for phones that don't work yet.

I think that finally succeeding at having a Linux phone is worth creating a post on HN. I was thinking about a Tell HN but decided to convert the knowledge into a repo so more people can share, discuss, add their phones, new apps, etc. Hope it helps!

name: Custom SQLites for agents (a remote MCP)
description:
What if your agents could create (almost) any SQLite database they need?

I built databasedmcp to let Claude (or any other agent) create databases for my sessions, in both Claude and Claude Code.

With the MCP, agents can create multiple databases with basically any schema.

Docs and tool descriptions: https://databasedmcp.com/docs

Some use cases that I've discovered:

* Share data between agents

Let agents store their status, what they're working on, etc. This is essentially about passing data between coding agents.

E.g. set up a worker agent that picks up work items that other agents add to the database. This kind of enables autonomous work discovery.

* Build custom apps

I've built many ad-hoc apps just by describing the idea to Claude. Ask it to create the UI as an artifact and to use databasedmcp as the backend.

Artifacts can call MCP tools however they want. You use the chat to modify the app, and use the app itself in the artifact UI.

Pretty easy to build small apps such as a shopping list, an expense tracker, etc. Then use Claude to extract data from documents, and store the data with databasedmcp in a structured manner.

Any comments are appreciated, thanks!

name: Ripcloc – cloc every edit your agent makes
description:
Hey HN.

ripcloc exists because I ask agents to consider line cost in feedback early and often when they're doing work to help constrain unnecessary complexity and to trigger discussions about code smells that lead to bad architecture.

It is fast enough that you can add it to a git commit hook. It is fast enough that your agent harness can run it after every tool call.

The other reason it exists is to help _count your tests_.

Ripcloc attributes each line as either a source line, a test line or a comment/doc line, so that you can have a better idea quickly how much your codebase is _implementation_ vs _tests_.

It does this even for inline tests like `#[cfg(test)] mod tests { ... }` in Rust (and is still faster than its predecessors!).

name: Craoli – find jobs without bias and manipulation from the platforms
description:
Hey HN, I have build a tool after my own job searching. You describe the job you want in a sentence, like "backend roles in Zurich, Python, no banks", and it searches the web and companies' own career pages for it. There is no bias, no curated lists, no promotion; only a pure and powerful search. I wanted to get the real postings. The same jobs can show up to many boards and recruiter sites, often after it's closed. Don't you want to know this? Craoli tries to find the employer's own postings, shows one card for all the copies that exist out there, and keeps checking whether the job is still open.

Another issue I had was that one company while I submitted my job application, changed the job description, by adding one more requirement that was not there when I have applied!! Good luck proving that. Of course the recruiter brought this point for my rejection, that I was sure that it was not there when I applied. 7+ years of pre-sales is hard to miss on a job description when read.

There are some limits for now; career pages are read directly only for the common hiring systems; a custom site is only found through web search. And every search costs me real money, so you need an account, and free has 2 searches a month using a cheaper LLM model; the search costs the same. Additional classical features are there for you to discover, like tailored CVs and cover letters.

What I would like to know: the last time you looked for a job, what made you stop trusting a listing?

name: Hubbub – Read big HN threads by topic
description:
Hi everyone!

Thank you all for the discussions here. They're the reason I visit and read HN every day.

Big threads are hard to follow. I wanted to see what people are actually talking about before diving in, so I had Opus 5.5 build me a Chrome extension.

On a thread page, Hubbub groups the top-level comments into a handful of topics, with a bar showing how much of the discussion each one takes up. Open a topic and you read the real comments btw, no AI summary. Haiku only groups comments, generates labels, and describes a topic in a sentence or two.

There's a live demo on the landing page: https://hubbub.page

How it works: a small server makes trees ahead of time for front-page threads with 30+ comments, and refreshes them as the threads grow. Every user downloads the same file, so the server can't tell which threads you read. There's no account and no analytics, and your read history stays in your browser.

Do give it a try, let me know if you spot any bugs, or have any feature requests :)

name: Jam – A music making game where you play gigs to earn studio gear
description:
The idea comes from Chrome Music Lab, which was addictive and satisfying. I felt it could be that fun and easy to put down musical ideas and hear them grow into something more substantial. Simple at first, but with progressively more depth if the player wants to go there. That was the seed, and it spiraled from there into Jam.

You start with one instrument, and you write parts on a piano roll. Create your own music or play gigs (levels) to earn coins and buy more gear. Each gig is built around one musical idea, so you pick up some music knowledge as you go. Friends can join your studio with a link and write parts alongside you.

In my other Show HNs I've always come with my own code. In this case I didn't write the code, but I'm still proud of the outcome and I hope some of you will enjoy it too.

The audio code is Rust/WASM running in a worklet. This is the part I had prior experience in, and it's been fun getting that into a browser. The instruments are decent and the signal chains hold their own. The front end is the agent's own design in three.js. The optimization work there was interesting because of how busy the UI gets and how many elements come into view. I focused on measuring React renders per interaction, instruction counts for the audio engine, load times and frame times. The result is something that runs decently even on a phone.

This simple setup allows collaborative music making out of the gate, even though it's not the game's main focus (yet).

name: Accounting built like Git, with files in your own storage
description:
Lots of ways to do your accounting today with LLMs, but for some reason there is this expectation you are suppose to keep the old accounting software around? And it sort of makes sense, they vouch for the ledger integrity and keep the audit trail.

It reminded me of how things where like before git. You trusted the host not just to keep the data but to vouch for the versioning, and what git really did was move that last part into the data itself.

Accounting ledgers need integrity, in fact it is mandated by law in most places. Git buys integrity by publishing, because if you do not share your repo with anyone, you can always force push and rewrite the commit history and no-one would know. But your books are sensitive and cannot be published.

So I made git-style versioning for double-entry accounting. Entries gets hashed and timestamped, service checks for debit equals credit, and it ends up as json files you keep in your own S3 bucket. Not in a vendor database. For the hosted version the access keys to the buckets are encrypted with the user passkey / assistant OAuth, so the service cannot read anything at-rest.

For user convenience there is a hosted version where you do the books through MCP on whatever LLM you already use. The whole thing is so cheap to run, because the service does not store any sensitive data, so it is free, although you need an AI client with MCP support and an S3 bucket.

Hosted version: https://bobalice.com Code walkthrough: https://bobalice.com/docs/alice

name: SwiphtNum 3.0 – native Mac statistics with SEM, SQL and scripting
description:
Hi HN, I build SwiphtNum, a statistics workspace written for the Mac in Swift, with the numeric kernels in C and Accelerate. There is no R or Python runtime inside; everything runs locally, and datasets never leave the machine.

What 3.0 changes:

- The SCL IDE. SCL is SwiphtNum's SPSS-like command language (169 commands). Scripts, SQL and results now share one window: any SQL statement is an SCL command, query results open in a Results tab, and the editor (a small C text engine) has autocomplete, folding, hover help and a command palette. SQLite, MySQL and PostgreSQL connect over SSL or SSH. - MANOVA: Pillai, Wilks, Hotelling and Roy, cell means, stepdown F and discriminant functions. - Ten interface languages, Text Size up to 200%, Differentiate Without Color and an Increase Contrast mode. - Statistical routines are tested against R and Python reference values in the test suite; the goldens are generated offline and checked in.

It also does CB-SEM and PLS-SEM on a visual canvas, 100+ procedures from one Analysis menu, APA 7 tables, and a spreadsheet with 191 Excel-compatible functions (dynamic arrays, LET, LAMBDA).

It needs macOS 14 or later and is a subscription ($4.99/month or $49.99/year, each with a free trial). Happy to answer anything about the stats engines, the SCL parser or the AppKit/SwiftUI split.

name: Stop applying to jobs using AI-generated resume
description:
When LLMs hands you a resume or pdf it carry markers of how it was made, including the source. You can't see them on the page but applicant tracking systems can read it.

So recruiters are flagging such profiles and rejecting them entirely. I had tested this across 40+ AI models (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Meta, etc) to produce a resume and every single file carried a marker.

To solve this problem. I had built a free tool to show what your file says and gives you a cleaned version:

- Drop your resume and get a cleaned copy - Free, no account.

What it doesn't do: it won't rewrite your resume or make AI-sounding wording more human. It only deals with what's hidden in the file.

It's a simple tool, but it feels absolutely necessary now as more people are using AI for generating their entire resume or even editing them. I am the developer, happy to answer any questions.

name: Musset, open-source Scrivener alternative with an AI that never writes
description:
I’m writing my first novel and could not find an app that fit my workflow: quiet like iA Writer, organized like Scrivener, and with AI so I can discuss my book while I write it. It allows me to feel less “alone” and have a sounding board while I write.

- A book is a folder of plain Markdown files. Musset commits to a git repo, tracks versions and drafts without you having to know git.

- Revisions are CriticMarkup inside the text. It manages docx revisions too, so your editor can edit a Word doc and you import their comments.

- PDFs are typeset using Typst, embedded in the app, following each language’s typographic rules.

- Spelling and grammar are checked using LanguageTool, also embedded.

name: Craoli – describe a job in one sentence, it finds real postings
description:
Hey HN, I have build a tool after my own job searching. You describe the job you want in a sentence, like "backend roles in Zurich, Python, no banks", and it searches the web and companies' own career pages for it. There is no bias, no curated lists, no promotion; only a pure and powerful search.

I wanted to get the real postings. The same jobs can show up to many boards and recruiter sites, often after it's closed. Don't you want to know this? Craoli tries to find the employer's own postings, shows one card for all the copies that exist out there, and keeps checking whether the job is still open.

Another issue I had was that one company while I submitted my job application, changed the job description, by adding one more requirement that was not there when I have applied!! Good luck proving that. Of course the recruiter brought this point for my rejection, that I was sure that it was not there when I applied. 7+ years of pre-sales is hard to miss on a job description when read.

There are some limits for now; career pages are read directly only for the common hiring systems; a custom site is only found through web search. And every search costs me real money, so you need an account, and free has 2 searches a month using a cheaper LLM model; the search costs the same. Additional classical features are there for you to discover, like tailored CVs and cover letters.

What I would like to know: the last time you looked for a job, what made you stop trusting a listing?

Board is a way to create, deploy, and fund a trading bot in 10 seconds. My co-founders and I built Board out of our own necessity. Every time we had a new trading strategy, we would need to manually input it into our broker accounts and monitor the situation ourselves.

We looked at all of our trading strategies over the past 3 years and added everything to the board that would be required to rebuild them from scratch. Now, when we have a new strategy, we chat with AI to create the strategy. We review the board to confirm that it matches what we expect, and we deploy it. We don't have to worry about setting up webhooks for signals or keeping it running on our computer locally.

The whole system is built on top of tokenized stocks and commodities. You always have access to withdraw your funds.

name: OpenComputer – an open source alternative to Devin
description:
Hi HN!

Utpal here, I'm one of the founders of OpenComputer.

OpenComputer is an open source cloud coding agent for teams that can run in your own cloud account (AWS, GCP, Azure).

We run the agent harness and the sandbox on the same durable VM (architecture in the docs [1]). First commit lands in 24s; the alternatives we benchmarked took 53-72s (benchmarks below [2]).

Two other choices:

- One VM per team, scalable horizontally. Sessions are isolated in git worktrees. - Session files are backed up to a repo after every turn, so any session can resume on another VM.

We noticed that past ~640 session-hours a month, one always-on 4 vCPU VM is cheaper than per-session E2B sandboxes, for example. So at scale, this setup would not only be faster than current SOTA coding agents, but also more cost-efficient.

Feel free to try via cloud for free [4] or self host. We would love any and all feedback, and happy to answer any questions! Full demo below [3].

[1]: https://docs.opencomputer.dev/getting-started/architecture [2]: https://opencomputer.dev/blog/cloud-agents-as-fast-as-local/ [3]: https://x.com/IgorZIJ/status/2121309785882591711 [4]: https://app.opencomputer.dev

description:
I've seen too many slow-log queries with a GROUP BY that makes Postgres blow up, so for the last two weeks or so I've been working on Straum. It leans on Postgres replication slots, logical or physical, to get its data. Postgres stays the source of truth.

I am ashamed to admit that I am one of those students who go to the library and get very little done (a.k.a. larping). It's very easy to get distracted if you have any electronic devices with you, but as a CS major, I can't just switch to pen and paper. That's why I started building this app called LarpLess with the help of a few friends.

LarpLess is a macOS/Windows app that checks your screen and camera with local AI to determine what you are studying or if you are distracted. Gives you a focus percentage at the end, with a breakdown of what you did during your session (Math, Physics, etc.)

Privacy is a big concern for an app like this, so it is open-source (AGPL 3.0) and uses locally run open-source models. It doesn't connect to the internet unless you want to check for updates or enable the friends feature (Disabled by default. You can make an account, add friends and see their shared study sessions/share your study sessions).

For the camera, it uses an object detection model, YOLO11n, to detect if there is a person and/or a phone at 1fps. For the screen, there are 2 options: the one we did first is reading window titles + a VLM on Ollama (default is qwen3-vl:2b), simple but power/RAM hungry. The one my friend added later can run on an average laptop easily. It takes less than a second for a verdict. It scores window titles + OCR text on the screen with MiniLM text embeddings and scores the screenshot with image embeddings using SigLIP 2. SigLIP 2 decides if the user is distracted, and MiniLM decides what they are working on. You can run the classifier-based mode on any modern laptop. If you want to use the VLM mode, you need a good GPU with enough VRAM (3GB+) to hold the model in it.

name: Nunya – A "digital privacy screen" that makes text illegible from afar
description:
Hello! I'm Marc.

I've built "Nunya", which is a sort of "digital privacy screen".

It redraws text to make it readable when looking at your monitor or phone from a normal distance, while making it hard to read by someone who might be looking over your shoulder.

It's based on “hybrid images” like the famous Einstein/Monroe image (from the paper at https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/1141911.1141919) and I thought it'd make a great way to mask text on your phone that you don't want someone nearby reading.

I particularly spent time on the transition - I wanted the text to be incredibly legible when close, but incredibly illegible when being far, and tried to optimise for a minimal transition between the two.

Demos can be seen at my site for it here: https://usenunya.com

I first released this over ten years ago as "PrivacyMessage" (my app names have definitely improved) when Apple first allowed iMessage apps. This was my first app geared towards the general market as I've spent the last 13 years developing iOS apps for a fairly niche market.

I'm happy to have brought it back as “Nunya”, and have currently made it available in three forms:

- Nunya for Messages (iPhone)

I first remade my iMessage app and gave it a bit more polish. It's free for 5 sends, and then $4.99 for a permanent unlock.

- Potfolio (iPhone)

I then figured Nunya would make for a great flagship feature in a "wealth tracking" finance app I was already working on, so anyone who might glance at your phone when on public transport can't quite see your bank balances. It's currently free (though I might add some new features with IAPs to it later).

- Nunya for Chrome

name: Online curling game/SIM with Three.js
description:
Hello!

One of my hobbies is curling in a league with the local curling club. From time to time, there's a setup of stones that is tricky and interesting to contemplate from a strategic perspective. A while back, I started working on a three.js-based curling simulator that would enable me to recreate situations from my league games and then try different shots.

As you may know, curling is notoriously tricky from a physics perspective. There are a variety of papers out there about this, including this one, which is one of the more recent dives into understanding why stones curl the way they do: https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-018-26595-y

Anyhow, with the help of Claude Code, I pulled together the work and converted the quick-and-dirty sim into a game you can play online. It's still a bit more of a sim than a game, perhaps, but it can be fun to play as a game.

Curling often is referred to as "chess on ice" because there's more strategy in choosing shots and playing ends than there would appear to be at first glance. The primary challenge of turning this into a game has been trying to figure out how to provide the computer player both with a policy for game and end-level strategy while also having it evaluate the tactical choices that have to be made for each shot.

For example, when would the computer try to blank (no points scored) an end deliberately so that it can retain hammer (last stone thrown) in the subsequent end? When should it throw a low vs. high center or corner guard in an attempt to make up a point deficit? When should it try to steal points from the hammer team vs. throwing protective stones that hold the hammer team to one point?

It's a fun side project for me, so I thought you all might enjoy giving it a shot. :)

name: HyprMac: Keyboard-driven tiling window manager for macOS
description:
HyprMac is an app organizer and workspace manager for macOS, inspired by Hyprland on Linux. Every time I open a new app, it instantly positions itself nicely in a tiled layout alongside my other apps on screen. By repurposing the Caps Lock key (who, let's face it, never got much use anyways) into the Hypr key, I now can use that one button to traverse across windows, swap apps around, switch workspaces, and a ton of other awesome stuff. If you ever forget a shortcut, Hypr + K shows you the whole list.

On top of that, there are a few extras I've come to rely on. An overview shows all your workspaces at once. A scratchpad holds apps you want nearby but out of the way. Apps that don't tile revert to the typical macOS behavior, which we call 'floating windows.' These sit on top of the tiled apps and are free to drag around on top of workspaces. It also features a real settings UI, accessible from the menu bar, so you don't spend time digging around for config files.

I'm a software developer and a macOS power user. For the last 15 years, I've pretty much only used a Mac for everything. I've tried Windows here and there, but these days I also have a Linux PC alongside my Mac. I went through a few distributions before I came across Omarchy (amazing distro btw), which uses Hyprland to automatically tile windows. By just learning a few shortcuts you can completely manage all your apps across a number of workspaces instantly. I fell in love, and I knew I had to have that experience on my Mac. I poked around at a few of the options, but none of them really did exactly what I had in mind. Thus, HyprMac was born.

To install HyprMac, follow the guide at https://hyprmac.app/guides/install/ (Homebrew or the DMG).

There is, though, the harsh reality of macOS. All window managers that keep SIP enabled, HyprMac included

name: Penumbra v2, an ergonomic colour scheme inspired by natural light
description:
Four years ago I shared v1 (https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=32348461), a low-contrast palette (high contrast options available) with daylight-inspired surfaces and equal-brightness syntax colours. Both colour appearance modelling and my understanding of it have moved forward since then, so I gave it a full revision using newer models, improving the execution across the board.

The background colours now follow a smooth transition of natural sunlight and shade throughout, with no more slight distortions to fit within the display's gamut.

The accent colours for syntax highlighting now compensate for the apparent glow of intense colours, properly fulfilling the promise of fluidly readable code while still allowing you to scan for tokens by hue.

I also overhauled the VS Code extension and expanded availability considerably (Neovim/Vim, Helix, Ghostty, Kitty, WezTerm, Alacritty, Sublime, iTerm2, and more).

name: Prediction market competition where only agents can trade
description:
Hi HN. I’ve been working on a project called Vaticin (with an i). Interested in your feedback.

Vaticin is a prediction market competition platform where only agents are allowed to make wagers. Humans can’t directly do so themselves. There’s no real-money wagering involved. Vaticin is built for competition, research, and education.

Every Monday morning, our LLM generates about 300 yes/no prediction questions across six categories: sports, finance, tech, entertainment, geopolitics, and science. The competition window runs Monday through Saturday, although some predictions won’t resolve for several weeks later. Agents take positions/allocations throughout the week, and then wagering locks on Saturday. Odds are live/dynamic and update with every new wager. Then a new competition cycle starts the next Monday.

We have a live leaderboard that refreshes as our LLM resolves prediction questions each night (with human moderation of resolutions).

Recognizing the value of existing prediction market competition platforms, we wanted to focus on forecasting models that are not only well-calibrated, but also make good market decisions and integrate game theory into their strategy. On Vaticin, agents have to decide which markets to take positions on, when to take a position, and how much to allocate. With the dynamic odds, agents have to adapt throughout the competition cycle. Vaticin measures more than raw prediction accuracy.

We built a few ways to build an agent. Beginners can use our no-code “agent builder” and choose which forecasting parameters/strategies they want to use, then Vaticin codes their agent, shows the user the code, but allows them to edit the code. I hope it will help beginners learn more about coding and AI agents. More experienced builders can connect their own agents through an API.

name: GhostFleet: A Battleship game with an advanced AI opponent
description:
Hi HN

I've always been drawn to puzzle and strategy games, and for a long time I've wanted to build a game of my own. While building my own version of battleship, I came across this idea of adding a super intelligent in-game AI which uses probability and statistics to reason with the board and fire its next shot.

The goal was to create a set of rules & logic capable of consistently outperforming human players, much like chess engines that have evolved to surpass even the world's strongest human chess players.

Thus I created WraithAI and named the game as Ghostfleet. WraithAI features:

1. Monte Carlo Simulation with Probability heatmaps: Before every turn WraithAI samples 800 possible enemy fleet configurations and aggregates them into a probability heatmap. It identifies the most likely locations of the enemy ships.

2. Bayesian Inference: After every shot it updates its beliefs and uses the information gain to draw a new heatmap. When two cells look equally likely WraithAI picks the one whose result would tell more about the hidden enemy fleet for its next turn.

3. Adaptive Strategy & defense: It adjusts its aggression based on the state of the game and has a mechanism which resists common search strategies.

I would genuinely like to know how people can find patterns in its behavior. Can you outsmart & beat WraithAI?

Ghostfleet also has multiplayer mode so you can play with your friends. There is a matchmaking component called TownSquare at the bottom through which you can share room codes with other players.

name: A collaborative music making game that teaches music as you play
description:
Jam is a music making game that runs in the browser. You start with one instrument, and you write parts on a piano roll. Create your own music or play gigs (levels) to ear coin and buy more gear. Each gig is built around one musical idea, so you pick up some music knowledge as you go. Friends can join your studio with a link and write parts alongside you.

In my other Show HNs I've always come with my own code. In this case I didn't write the code, but I'm still proud of the outcome and I hope some of you will enjoy it too.

The audio code is Rust/WASM running in a worklet. This is the part I had prior experience in, and it's been fun getting that into a browser. The instruments are decent and the signal chains hold their own. The front end is the agent's own design in three.js. The optimization work there was interesting because of how busy the UI gets and how many elements come into view. I focused on measuring React renders per interaction, instruction counts for the audio engine, load times and frame times. The result is something that runs decently even on a phone.

This is a beta: feedback, comments and criticisms are all welcome. You can get into the game with no signup, and if you want to save your progress you'll be prompted to enter an email address.

description:
Hi everyone, Alex here - I’m one of the founders of ThunderPhone. We’re excited to announce the launch of Zeus, a platform that makes AI phone calls actually work without extensive hand-tuning!

A (somewhat long) summary:

When we started building business phone agents in 2024, we kept running into technical problems that ruined calls, caused by the limits of existing architectures. The two biggest issues were that phone agents misheard callers, and disobeyed scripts or responded in weird ways.

Both stemmed from the prevailing voice agent architecture - a “three-step” or “cascaded” pipeline: one transcription model turning caller audio into text, one LLM generating a response (and sometimes tool calls) from that text, and a TTS model turning response text into audio.

Transcription models aren’t perfect, especially in noisy environments, with unclear callers, in languages other than English, and on short utterances like “yeah”. With the pipeline approach, when caller audio is boiled down to a single “best guess” text transcript, mistakes are often unrecoverable: there’s typically no “top n” best guesses or other audio signal for the LLM to use if the transcript was wrong. That leads the LLM to respond to what the transcription model thought it heard instead of what the caller actually said.

The pipeline approach also caused weird responses and poor instruction-following due to the tradeoff between LLM speed and intelligence. Phone calls demand fast responses to feel natural, which is in tension with an LLM’s need to “think” and run inference - often for several seconds - to answer many prompts correctly. name: erXos – a microkernel OS in Erlang based on Genera/Plan 9/QNX ideas
description:
What if every Erlang process were an operating-system process? With as much system code and drivers written in Erlang itself. This is something I was pondering for a while, and finally was able to prototype thanks to AI coding agents.

erXos is a capability-based microkernel OS in Erlang: drivers, filesystems, and the network stack are all supervised Erlang processes, same as any app.

The kernel itself is Fiasco, in C++, slightly modified for erXos needs. This is an OS I wanted for a long time: an Erlang machine where every BEAM process is a process visible to the OS and scheduler, not something bolted on top.

You can try it right now with nothing to install: there is an emulator on the website that boots the whole OS in the browser ARM64 emulator. At the rc prompt, try `ps`, `top`, `ping` or `erl` and write any kind of erlang code. There's a Pi 4 SD image and a QEMU image too. The goal is to build an ultra-reliable microkernel OS with hot code loading and both system and BEAM-based isolation. The latter is one thing that would allow you to run millions of processes on the system, something that would be prohibitive on a microkernel alone due to the context switch overhead. Capabilities keep every component least-privileged, supervision keeps the machine running when drivers or subsystems crash, and hot code loading would let you fix a broken driver without reboot.

The secondary goal is to keep as much of a UNIX face as possible. Too many novel OSes change things for no particular reason that makes them hard to use. erXos tries to preserve as many existing UNIX/FreeBSD concepts as much as possible to remove the learning curve.

What works today:

- Boots in the browser/v64, in QEMU, and on a Raspberry Pi 4 from an SD card

- A real shell (plan9 rc) with job control, pipes, `ps`, `grep`. It feels like UNIX on the surface

name: Bocalito – A Meal Prep Planner
description:
I started to meal prep a few months ago, and loved it because it saves me time and frees my mind. Also I spend way less ordering food when I don't know what to eat, which is often. But I got tired of looking for recipes in books and websites that I could not adapt to myself.

And I had to go back and forth 1000 times on rebuilding prompts every time.

I am a developer, so I decided to build a tool on my own, for myself, trying to fix in code what AI keeps getting wrong: I left AI do the creative part, and the code take care of reliability. And it keeps getting better, since it has been evolving ever since.

Finally I decided to make this Free App to see if other people wanted to try it and if it would solve the same issue for anyone else.

Any feedback is appreciated, and if you meal prep, I hope you like it!

name: Billet – 6MB (Agentic) Task Management System
description:
Ever since AI has come, I've got worse at managing project tasks / goals. When you develop so fast now, things start lacking behind. For that reason I looked into creating a good set of skills I can use in any agent that support skills.

The result is billet-skills which you can find at https://github.com/Skytrias/billet-skills

Tasks are Markdown files with JSON frontmatter that live in docs/tasks/:

    ---
    { "id": 7, "title": "Add dark mode", "status": "ready", ... }
    ---
    ## Outcome
    The app follows the system's light or dark setting.
This allows me to create a bunch of tasks upfront and work on things more easily or in parallel.

Billet comes in two parts:

1. billet-skills, the skills: https://github.com/Skytrias/billet-skills

2. Billet, the viewer https://mktwsk.xyz/billet

Billet has a few ways of looking at the tasks in your project:

- List Mode

- Kanban Mode

- Plan Mode

Multiple Projects can be seen in the Home Dashboard and also a simple Timeline.

You can change the skills to whatever you like as long as it conforms to the format.

Other than that thats pretty much it. I've also got easy copy&paste support so it becomes easier saying "work on X and Y".

Billet is free - Give it a try and have fun! Feedback is welcome :)

Billet itself is closed-source though - as I have commercial projects that use the same UI core.

---

For those interested in the tech:

- Software Rendered UI, using Blend2D

- Custom immediate mode UI

- Custom platform layer

- Made in Odin

name: Wikipedia Current Event Portal as an Actual Newspaper (and in RSS)
description:
I wanted to diversify the sources of my RSS feeds, and realized the Wikipedia Current Events portal (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portal:Current_events) contains events that sometimes other sources missed.

I decided to create an RSS feed for it, but after a while I realized the entries are sometimes too long and are truncated in the RSS title, and some entries don't have a proper article linked to them so it was not possible to properly render a title and link for each RSS feed.

So I ended up creating a web portal to check the news. The site is static and updates around 2 times a day.

I added some nice features like crawling the linked sources and showing the original news websites title and image (this only works if the site provides og: tags and accepts connections from crawlers), and grouping related articles visually.

Hope you find this useful, or at least, interesting.

As attributed in the footer of the page:

"Unofficial project, not affiliated with the Wikimedia Foundation. The text comes from Wikipedia contributors and is available under the CC BY-SA 4.0 license; every entry links to the source article and its page history."

name: Relic – An AI that only answers from what you've saved
description:
Hi HN, I’m Imran, one of 3 founders building Relic AI

We started building Relic because we constantly experienced the problem of saving a lot of resources online such as websites, PDFs, Youtube videos and podcasts, but when we actually needed any of them, we couldn’t find them because they were burried in various places.

We were saving stuff in open tabs, bookmarks, watch later lists and folders. But retrieving them when it mattered was a real problem for us. We spent a lot of time digging through our saves and redoing research that was already done just to find that one thing that we needed.

So we decided to build a tool that helps you easily save resources, organizes them automatically and helps you find what you need when you need it.

Relic lets you save web pages, PDFs, Youtube videos, notes, import bookmarks and open tabs, integrates with Notion and Google drive, and it even has an MCP so that you can conect it to AI tools you already use.

We also have an AI chat inside Relic that only answers from your own saved resources with citations.

Our free beta has been open since October and we want to hear as much feedback as possible.

name: Fdroid Feed Manager and API
description:
Hi guys. I had an idea to wrote API and some nice WebUI for Fdroid private feed for Android APKs for quite some time. I have some internal applications that I want to share with my family (i.e. smart home management app). First I had just bunch of static files that were managed by my GitLab instance but at some point it broke.

Then with growing number of applications and packages and no possibility of managing them easily (I think Fdroid tools are unnecessarily complicated) it was too much to do by hand. With coding agents I decided to try it out and write an application entirely by agent (as kind of experiment) it was usable but quite buggy. And costly.

After that I fixed bugs with local model, cleaned up code, added tests, tested it for few weeks myself with Fdroid clients on multiple phones and other devices. It is working and I decided to share it with community.

It us an API wrapping Fdroid python packages for managing Fdroid feed, signing APKs and etc. It supports API keys that I am feeding to my CI to upload new APKs after the build. It allows to:

- add, update and remove applications

- manages their keys so you do not have to

- allows to add description and icons

- allows to add (with release changes) and remove releases of applications

- manages versions of next release

It is designed to be integrated with SSO of your choice, because having SSO for your self hosted applications seems much better idea than each of local applications to manage it itself.

Links:

https://github.com/npodbielski/FdroidManager

https://hub.docker.com/r/npodbielski/fdroidmgr/tags

I hope it can be of use for more people.

name: Orbital – Everything (known) in Earth orbit, live in 3D, in the browser
description:
I look up a lot at the sky at night and made this because I wanted to better understand what is up there.

Orbital shows all 32,000+ tracked objects at their current positions: about 17,000 working satellites, 2,800 dead ones, 2,200 spent rocket bodies and 10,700 pieces of debris.

Each is color coded, can be switched off, and can be "clicked" to follow. For the well-known ones it pulls up a real photo (where available), what it is for, and when it stopped working.

There is an animation that shows launch history from 1957 to today. When you first visit, click on the "Watch 1957 → today" button to see the animation.

You can also "fly out" to the solar system and see the planets, moons, comets and spacecraft further out there.

My orbit data comes from Space-Track. I also pull from CelesTrak to determine which satellites are currently active.

It is a static site on GitHub Pages (currently) with no backend, no accounts, and no ads. It also installs as an app and reopens offline.

I wrote it with Claude Code doing most of the implementation. I will provide the link to the source if you want it.

I would like to hear what you think about it. Specifically, what is confusing on a first visit, and what would make you come back to it. And anything else constructive you would like to share.

description:
Hello! Looking to share forbear, a immediate mode GUI library that looks like the web, has a React-like DX and is as fast as possible.

On Linux and macOS:

  curl -fsSL https://forbear.dev/quick-start.sh | sh
On Windows:

  irm https://www.forbear.dev/quick-start.ps1 | iex
It's missing basic features like accessibility, input method support, and built-in text input primitives.

It has a LICENSE that makes it source available. It's free for nonprofits, open source software or internal tools, but, it charges a capped 1% royalty for any company that exceeds a revenue threshold.

I would love to hear feedback, specially on the new C API as I am not very experienced with C.

Thanks!

name: Local Graph for Your Agents
description:

How do I use it: 1. I've scanned all my documents and stored passports, driver licences and all kind of contracts for my apartment, insurance and so on. And not only mine - the entire family. 2. So i can ask "give me a passport number of my son" and it gives it back instantly. It might not be a big deal, but it is very convenient. 3. It stores all the projects I'm working on, key steps and decisions. 4. And the most important thing - it works from anywhere. I can ask Hermes i telegram to remind me when my insurance ends or I can reference my project in ClaudeCode just by name and it will get the entire history from Antigravity.

I would be happy if you guys find it useful.

name: It's Raining Somewhere – hear live simulated weather anywhere on Earth
description:
I like listening to rain and I like maps, so I built a physics-based simulator of how rain sounds on different surfaces and linked it up to a live weather map.

You can pick any place on the map and play what the rain there would sound like right now, driven by live weather data. It grew into a whole soundscape: thunder, wind, seasonally appropriate birds, insects, frogs, the sea, vehicles and other urban sounds. The sound is binaural, so with headphones it has some spatial depth.

Only the birds are recordings (from xeno-canto, with attribution). Every other environmental sound is synthesized in your browser by a C++ engine compiled WebAssembly.

There's also a live radio that tunes to real local stations near wherever you are on the map. It gets mixed with the environmental sounds and you can adjust it to sound like it's coming from far away. Nearby storms can add crackle to the radio signal.

The radar map comes from my own tile server. It uses raw public radar data where available and falls back to satellite otherwise.

I'd love to hear feedback!

name: Cashcraft – free precise budgeting without categories
description:
Hi HN! I'm Matthew, a software engineer tired of paid budgeting apps doing fuzzy averages and making me categorize every card swipe.

Example: which category is Rent on the 1st? Which category is my $114 "Valuemart" purchase last week? It doesn't matter IMO. What matters is that Rent repeats every 1st, I have $218 left for spending until Friday, and I can contribute $500 to my Roth IRA next paycheck and have $2,000 left in that account.

Bills just cost what they cost, and I need to see exactly when they will come out and how much money that leaves me on that day.

For spending, I just move a hunk of cash to a separate "safe to spend" account every Friday and try not to blow through it. This means I can see exactly when spending money will come out too, and how much money that leaves me. I might spend more on gas this week and more for the party next week; there's no 'normal' week. It sounds simple, but it took me years of trial and error to find this system that consistently works for me and make a halfway-decent app to track it.

Cashcraft is free, and doesn't require an account to start locally. If you do sign up, your data is end-to-end encrypted. Bank sync is built but not public yet, because it costs money via Plaid, but you can import transactions from your bank. I might add it as a paid feature later. I wish bank sync could be free, but integrating with 100s of legacy bank systems necessarily costs Plaid money, which makes them charge implementers money.

If you're interested, give it a try and let me know what you like or don't about it. I'd like to improve it. Thank you!

name: Fast deterministic natural language search for OpenStreetMap data
description:
I want to show you HippoMaps. It is a fully featured map and navigation app built on OpenStreetMap with a custom Overpass API engine for really fast search of POIs, areas and ways.

My aim with HippoMaps is to get to a level where I don't need Google Maps anymore. The biggest hurdle IMHO with OSM based apps is the lack of nice and fast search (where GMaps excels at). To get there I started working on a deterministic (as in no LLMs used) parser of queries that translates them to the Overpass QL.

Search queries are split into tokens and the algorithm tries to guess "what" you want to search and "where". The former comes from a word list (known brands, sports, OSM tags) and the latter from the geocoder service (Photon).

You can get quite creative like "cafes in Zurich by the Limmat", "peaks over 4000 m in Valais", "pharmacies open now in Bern". It's good for discovering hiking trails, e.g. "hiking trails from Arth-Goldau to Rigi Kulm". It knows how to find stuff between two places, next to a place, near a place and so on. You can stack those as well like "bridges over the danube in serbia 50 km from novi sad".

Except the search it has almost all of the features you would expect from a map like turn-by-turn navigation (Valhalla) with voice (Piper), public transport navigation in Europe (MOTIS), live traffic (only a few countries so far).

The app is GPL-3.0: https://github.com/cdutsov/hippomaps

I'm looking forward to feedback on searches that work or don't work for you + overall comments.

name: Openspot – macOS launcher for disposable tools
description:
Hi HN! We're Tony, Kolom and Anastasiia, a small team from Ukraine.

Today we are open-sourcing Openspot, our research project on using generative UI in day-to-day work.

The idea is simple: generate a tool (spot) for your current task using coding agent, and keep it if you like it or remove it after use if you don't. We are using Openspot daily and really enjoying the possibilities it unlocks. Some examples of spots:

- caffeinate, which allows the Mac to work with the lid closed

- local file and screenshot search in natural language using EmbeddingGemma 2

- draw on screen during calls or before screenshots

- AI agents monitoring

- AirDrop, but over the network (using iroh)

We built it because of two things:

1. Over the past year, we (and almost every designer and engineer we know) have started making small tools using coding agents. But the DX for macOS applications is very frustrating even for coders, and you have to pay for a developer account to share them.

2. And we kind of miss the days of custom Winamp skins and Twitter clients. That's why every part of Openspot is customizable, so anyone can give it their own look and feel.

This is a very early stage. The code is MIT-licensed, and the core will remain free forever. We're sticking to macOS 26+ for now (because of Liquid Glass).

Ask us anything, or roast it. Any feedback is very appreciated.

name: Purple Flow – AI-first n8n alternative, 10k+ workflows on 512MB
description:
Hey all! I ran into a wall with n8n - hard and expensive to scale, limited streaming, heavy MCP is confusing for agents.

That scaling was becoming more and more critical as I was beginning to build agentic swarms. So I built my own alternative with Elixir and Beam. Been using it in production for almost 2 months.

It connects my agent to multiple databases, sandboxes, and APIs. I've even migrated over my most used n8n workflows without a hiccup.

I ran some benchmarks and 10,000 concurrent workflows executed in 3 seconds and cost about 330MB of ram (listed as 512 in the case study). Equivalent workflows in n8n took 2GB of ram to run 100. It's roughly 200x the memory efficiency of the usual Node/Python stacks. And while you don't edit the workflows yourself visually, you can see and manage them through a UI, along with credentials that the agent never sees.

The workflows themselves are pure TOML. Not as easy as dragging node connectors. But the idea is that AI creates the flows and you can easily understand them.

This isn't a shaky demo. I'm using it as my daily driver to create complex multi-agent personas, run research and info gathering swarms, and whatever else my agent needs to get its job done. (it's built more than 70 so far)

I have a live working demo on my website that was built by an agent using Purple Flow to connect to my server. The demo itself lets an agent using Purple Flow access live (Adventure Works) data and generate reports, documents, and slides on demand. My agent and I built it in an afternoon. It runs on a lightweight model (to save money for a public demo) with very few hiccups.

- Repo: https://github.com/leetheguy/purple_flow - Discord, benchmarks, and demo links in the repo.

name: Run CalculiX, OpenFOAM and ParaView jobs on your office's idle PCs
description:
OmnibusCloud aims to join different user devices into a single computing engine, which I call the Ultracomputer. Today it works with Windows, Linux, or Mac OS (ARM) computers. Next, it will be able to connect smartphones, tablets, game consoles, and any other computing device.

It is no secret that most of our computers spend most of their lives idle, and there have been attempts to use this idle power before. The most famous of them is BOINC. But OmnibusCloud, following the first part of its name, is trying to provide a system that will be easy to use for any actors.

OmnibusCloud is splitting tasks into chunks and distributing them to machines available to you. Each machine processes its own chunk individually and then sends back the result.

Today, OmnibusCloud is introducing simulation tools:

- ParaView plugin allows users to render engineering animations, similar to render farms like SheepIt does for Blender, on machines in your group

- PrePoMax solver replacement can distribute thermal analysis tasks to machines in your group

- WitSweep can plan and run hundreds of FEA (with CalculiX solver) or CFD (with OpenFOAM solver) cases in one click; you can schedule your research that will start on your office machines when everyone is at home, and then in the morning you will get the results.

OmnibusCloud works on a crowdcomputing model, similar to crowdfunding, but with computer power instead of money. The one who needs computation can open a project, and users can join it.

Today we are just launching the public beta, so there are very few users and machines, so to try our system, it will be better to start with a Private Group. Create your own group and invite your friends or team (or connect your office workstation) - you will get your own subnetwork to run your tasks.

Check our repositories: https://github.com/OmnibusCloud
